docs.title: 📖 What is Angular Architecture?
docs.text:
Angular follows a component-based architecture, where an application is divided into reusable building blocks.

These building blocks include:

  • Components
  • Services
  • Directives
  • Pipes
  • Dependency Injection
  • Routing
  • Modules / Standalone Components

Together, they help build scalable, maintainable, and testable Single Page Applications (SPA).

docs.title: 🧩 Angular Building Blocks
docs.text: Building Block Purpose Component Builds UI Service Business logic & API calls Directive Changes DOM behavior Pipe Formats data Routing Navigation Dependency Injection Provides objects automatically Module Groups related functionality

docs.title: What is a Component?
docs.text:
A component is the basic building block of Angular.

Every screen in Angular consists of one or more components.

Example:

App
│
├── Header
├── Sidebar
├── Product List
│      ├── Product Card
│      ├── Product Card
│      └── Product Card
└── Footer

Each component contains:

  • HTML
  • CSS / SCSS
  • TypeScript
  • @Component decorator

Example

@Component({
  selector: 'app-home',
  templateUrl: './home.component.html'
})
export class HomeComponent {}

docs.title: Why Components?
docs.text:
• Reusable
  • Easy to maintain
  • Independent
  • Easier testing

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Services contain business logic.

❌ Bad

Component
   │
HTTP Call

✅ Good

Component
   │
Service
   │
HttpClient
   │
Backend

Example

@Injectable({
  providedIn:'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {

   getEmployees(){
      return this.http.get('/employees');
   }

}

docs.title: Directives
docs.text: Directives change the behavior of HTML.

docs.title: Structural Directives
docs.text:
• *ngIf
  • *ngFor
  • *ngSwitch

They add or remove DOM elements.

Example

<div *ngIf="isLoggedIn">

docs.title: Attribute Directives
docs.text:
• ngClass
  • ngStyle

They modify an existing element.

Example

<!-- Legacy approach -->
<div [ngClass]="{ 'is-active': active }"></div>
<div [ngStyle]="{ 'background-color': statusColor }"></div>

<!-- Modern approach -->
<div [class.is-active]="active"></div>
<div [style.background-color]="statusColor"></div>

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
Pipes transform data before displaying it.

Example

{{ salary | currency }}

Common Pipes

  • date
  • uppercase
  • lowercase
  • currency
  • percent
  • json

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Instead of creating objects manually,

EmployeeService service = new EmployeeService();

Angular automatically injects them.

constructor(private employeeService: EmployeeService){}

Benefits

  • Loose coupling
  • Easy testing
  • Reusability

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Angular is a Single Page Application.

Routing maps URLs to components.

/home
     ↓
HomeComponent

/dashboard
      ↓
DashboardComponent

docs.title: Why should API calls be in Services?
Difference between Modules and Standalone Components.
2-Minute Interview Answer
docs.text: Angular follows a component-based architecture where the UI is divided into reusable components. Components are responsible for presentation, while services contain business logic and API communication. Angular uses Dependency Injection to provide services automatically. Routing enables navigation between views without page reloads. Modules or Standalone Components organize the application, while directives and pipes extend HTML and format data. The application starts from index.html, executes main.ts, bootstraps Angular, loads the root component, fetches data through services, and updates the UI using change detection.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Angular is component-based.
  • Components build UI.
  • Services contain business logic.
  • Dependency Injection manages object creation.
  • Routing enables SPA navigation.
  • Directives modify HTML.
  • Pipes transform data.
  • Change Detection keeps the UI synchronized with data.

docs.title: 📖 What are Lifecycle Hooks?
docs.text:
A component lifecycle is the sequence of stages an Angular component goes through from its creation to its destruction.

Angular provides Lifecycle Hooks, which are special methods that allow developers to execute custom logic at different stages of a component's life.

Common use cases include:

  • Initializing data
  • Responding to input changes
  • Accessing child components
  • Performing custom change detection
  • Cleaning up subscriptions

docs.title: Component Lifecycle Flow
docs.text:
Component Created
       │
       ▼
constructor()
       │
       ▼
ngOnChanges()
       │
       ▼
ngOnInit()
       │
       ▼
ngDoCheck()
       │
       ▼
ngAfterContentInit()
       │
       ▼
ngAfterContentChecked()
       │
       ▼
ngAfterViewInit()
       │
       ▼
ngAfterViewChecked()
       │
       ▼
(Repeated Change Detection)
       │
       ▼
ngOnDestroy()

docs.title: Complete Lifecycle Order
docs.text: Order Hook Called Once? Purpose 1 constructor ✅ Create component instance 2 ngOnChanges ❌ Detect @Input changes 3 ngOnInit ✅ Initialize component 4 ngDoCheck ❌ Custom change detection 5 ngAfterContentInit ✅ Content projection initialized 6 ngAfterContentChecked ❌ Projected content checked 7 ngAfterViewInit ✅ View initialized 8 ngAfterViewChecked ❌ View checked 9 ngOnDestroy ✅ Cleanup resources

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The constructor is a TypeScript feature, not an Angular lifecycle hook.

Angular calls it when creating the component instance.

constructor(private employeeService: EmployeeService) {}

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Dependency Injection
  • Simple property initialization

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• API calls
  • DOM manipulation
  • Business logic

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text: The constructor is used only for object creation and dependency injection. Initialization logic should be placed in ngOnInit().

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called whenever an @Input() property changes.

It is also called before ngOnInit() during the first initialization.

@Input() employee!: Employee;

ngOnChanges(changes: SimpleChanges) {
    console.log(changes);
}

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Refresh child component data
  • Compare previous and current values
  • Trigger calculations

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
When is ngOnChanges called?

Answer

  • Before ngOnInit() (initial binding)
  • Every time an @Input() value changes

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called once after Angular initializes all input properties.

ngOnInit() {

}

docs.title: Common Uses
docs.text:
• API calls
  • Initialize forms
  • Load dropdown data
  • Subscribe to Observables
  • Set default values

docs.title: Real Project Example
docs.text:
ngOnInit() {
   this.loadProjects();
   this.loadEnergyTypes();
}

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text: Most initialization code belongs here.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called during every Angular change detection cycle.

Allows developers to implement custom change detection.

ngDoCheck() {

}

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Detect deep object changes
  • Manual comparison

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text: Heavy computations because this hook executes frequently.

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
When would you use ngDoCheck?

Answer:

Only when Angular's default change detection is insufficient.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called after Angular projects external content using <ng-content>.

<app-card>
    <h2>Hello</h2>
</app-card>

<!-- app-card -->
<ng-content></ng-content>

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Access projected content
  • Initialize projected templates

docs.title: 6. ngAfterContentChecked()
docs.text:
Called every time projected content is checked.

Usually not used unless custom monitoring is required.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called after Angular initializes the component's view and child views.

Useful with:

  • ViewChild
  • ViewChildren
@ViewChild('inputBox')
input!: ElementRef;

ngAfterViewInit() {
   this.input.nativeElement.focus();
}

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Focus an input
  • Initialize charts
  • Access child components
  • Integrate third-party libraries

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
Why not access ViewChild inside ngOnInit?

Answer:

Because the view has not been created yet.

docs.title: 8. ngAfterViewChecked()
docs.text:
Called after every change detection cycle for the component's view.

Avoid heavy logic because it executes frequently.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Called just before Angular destroys the component.

ngOnDestroy() {

}

docs.title: Common Uses
docs.text:
• Unsubscribe Observables
  • Remove event listeners
  • Stop timers
  • Disconnect WebSockets

Example

subscription!: Subscription;

ngOnDestroy() {
   this.subscription.unsubscribe();
}

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
Why is ngOnDestroy important?

Answer:

To prevent memory leaks by cleaning up resources.

docs.text:
User opens page
      │

docs.title: Real Project Example
docs.text: Suppose your application has an Employee List page.

docs.title: constructor()
docs.text:
Inject services.

constructor(private employeeService: EmployeeService) {}

docs.title: ngOnInit()
docs.text:
Load employee data.

ngOnInit() {
   this.loadEmployees();
}

docs.title: ngOnChanges()
docs.text: Reload data when selected department changes.

docs.title: ngAfterViewInit()
docs.text: Focus the search box automatically.

docs.title: ngOnDestroy()
docs.text: Unsubscribe from WebSocket updates.

docs.title: What is the order of Angular Lifecycle Hooks?
docs.text:
constructor
↓
ngOnChanges
↓
ngOnInit
↓
ngDoCheck
↓
ngAfterContentInit
↓
ngAfterContentChecked
↓
ngAfterViewInit
↓
ngAfterViewChecked
↓
ngOnDestroy

docs.title: Difference between constructor and ngOnInit
docs.text: constructor ngOnInit TypeScript feature Angular lifecycle hook Dependency Injection Initialization logic Called during object creation Called after input properties are initialized Avoid API calls Best place for API calls

docs.title: Difference between ngOnChanges and ngOnInit
docs.text: ngOnChanges ngOnInit Runs whenever an @Input() changes Runs only once Receives SimpleChanges No parameters Can run multiple times Runs once after first ngOnChanges

docs.title: Which hooks run multiple times?
docs.text:
• ngOnChanges
  • ngDoCheck
  • ngAfterContentChecked
  • ngAfterViewChecked

docs.title: Which hooks run only once?
docs.text:
• constructor
  • ngOnInit
  • ngAfterContentInit
  • ngAfterViewInit
  • ngOnDestroy

docs.title: Common Interview Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Calling APIs inside the constructor.

❌ Accessing @ViewChild in ngOnInit().

❌ Forgetting to unsubscribe in ngOnDestroy().

❌ Performing expensive computations in ngDoCheck().

❌ Confusing ngOnChanges() with ngOnInit().

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The constructor is for dependency injection and object creation.
  • ngOnInit() is the preferred place for initialization logic and API calls.
  • ngOnChanges() responds to changes in @Input() properties.
  • ngAfterViewInit() is the right place to access @ViewChild.
  • ngOnDestroy() prevents memory leaks by cleaning up resources.
  • Understanding the order and purpose of lifecycle hooks is a common interview expectation for Angular developers.

docs.title: 📖 What is Data Binding?
docs.text:
Data Binding is the mechanism that synchronizes data between the Component (TypeScript) and the Template (HTML).

It allows Angular to automatically update the UI when the component data changes and update the component when the user interacts with the UI.

Without Data Binding, developers would have to manually update the DOM using JavaScript.

docs.title: Why Do We Need Data Binding?
docs.text:
Suppose we have:

username = "Jyothi";

Without Angular Data Binding:

document.getElementById("name").innerText = username;

Every time username changes, we must manually update the DOM.

With Angular:

<h2>{{ username }}</h2>

Angular automatically updates the UI whenever username changes.

docs.title: How Data Binding Works
docs.text:
Component (TypeScript)
                    │
         -------------------------
         │                       │
         ▼                       ▼
    Component Data          Component Events
         │                       ▲
         ▼                       │
            Angular Data Binding
         ▲                       │
         │                       ▼
      HTML Template (View)

Angular keeps the Component and Template synchronized.

docs.title: Types of Data Binding
docs.text:
Angular supports four types of Data Binding.

Binding Type Direction Syntax Interpolation Component ➜ View {{ value }} Property Binding Component ➜ View [property]="value" Event Binding View ➜ Component (event)="method()" Two-Way Binding Component ⇄ View [(ngModel)]="value"

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Interpolation displays data from the component in the template.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
{{ expression }}

Example

name = "Jyothi";

<h1>{{ name }}</h1>

Output

Jyothi

docs.title: What Can We Use?
docs.text:
Variables

{{ name }}

Expressions

{{ 10 + 20 }}

Function calls

{{ getFullName() }}

Ternary operators

{{ isAdmin ? 'Admin' : 'User' }}

docs.title: Can we write loops inside interpolation?
docs.text:
No.

Interpolation only supports expressions.

This is invalid:

{{ for(...) }}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Simple expressions only

❌ Heavy calculations

❌ API calls

❌ Long-running functions

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Property Binding sends data from the component to an HTML element property.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
[property]="expression"

Example

imageUrl = "assets/profile.png";

<img [src]="imageUrl">

Angular updates the src property whenever imageUrl changes.

docs.title: More Examples
docs.text:
Disable button

isDisabled = true;

<button [disabled]="isDisabled">

Set placeholder

<input [placeholder]="username">

Dynamic class

<div [class.active]="isActive">

Dynamic style

<div [style.color]="textColor">

docs.title: Attribute Binding vs Property Binding
docs.text:
Property Binding

<input [disabled]="true">

Attribute Binding

<input [attr.colspan]="2">

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
Property Binding updates DOM properties.

Attribute Binding updates HTML attributes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Event Binding allows the template to notify the component when an event occurs.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
(event)="method()"

Example

<button (click)="save()">

Component

save(){
   console.log("Saved");
}

docs.title: Common Events
docs.text:
• click
  • input
  • change
  • blur
  • focus
  • keyup
  • keydown
  • submit

docs.title: Passing Event Object
docs.text:
<input (input)="onInput($event)">

onInput(event:any){
   console.log(event.target.value);
}

docs.title: Real Project Example
docs.text:
Search box

<input
    (keyup)="searchEmployees($event)">

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Synchronizes data between the component and the view.

Changes in either place automatically update the other.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
[(ngModel)]="username"

Example

username = "";

<input [(ngModel)]="username">

<h3>{{ username }}</h3>

Typing inside the input automatically updates the component.

Updating the component automatically updates the input.

docs.title: Internal Working
docs.text:
Two-Way Binding is a combination of:

Property Binding

[value]="username"

+

Event Binding

(input)="username=$event.target.value"

Equivalent to

[(ngModel)]="username"

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text:
Must import

FormsModule

Otherwise Angular throws:

Can't bind to 'ngModel'

docs.title: One-Way vs Two-Way Binding
docs.text: One-Way Two-Way Component → View Component ⇄ View Faster Slightly more overhead Preferred for display Used in forms

docs.title: Real Project Example
docs.text:
Employee Search

searchText = "";

<input [(ngModel)]="searchText">

<table>

<tr *ngFor="let emp of employees">

User types

↓

Component updates

↓

Filter runs

↓

Table refreshes automatically

docs.title: Data Binding Flow
docs.text:
Component
    │
    ▼
Data Binding
    │
    ▼
HTML View

User Interaction
    │
    ▼
Event Binding
    │
    ▼
Component Updated
    │
    ▼
Change Detection
    │
    ▼
Updated UI

docs.title: What is Data Binding?
docs.text: Data Binding synchronizes data between the Component and the View.

docs.title: How many types of Data Binding are there?
docs.text:
Four

  • Interpolation
  • Property Binding
  • Event Binding
  • Two-Way Binding

docs.title: Difference between Interpolation and Property Binding
docs.text: Interpolation Property Binding Displays text Sets DOM properties {{ }} [ ] Mostly for text Used for HTML properties

docs.title: Difference between Property Binding and Event Binding
docs.text: Property Binding Event Binding Component → View View → Component [ ] ( )

docs.title: What is Two-Way Binding?
docs.text:
Two-Way Binding keeps the component property and UI synchronized.

Implemented using:

[(ngModel)]

docs.title: How does Two-Way Binding work internally?
docs.text:
It combines:

[value]

and

(input)

docs.title: Why is FormsModule required?
docs.text: Because ngModel belongs to FormsModule.

docs.title: Common Interview Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using interpolation inside HTML attributes

<img src="{{image}}">

Preferred

<img [src]="image">

❌ Forgetting FormsModule

❌ Writing heavy functions inside interpolation

{{ calculateSalary() }}

Runs during every change detection cycle.

❌ Confusing Property Binding with Attribute Binding

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Data Binding synchronizes the Component and Template.
  • Angular provides four types of Data Binding.
  • Interpolation displays text.
  • Property Binding updates DOM properties.
  • Event Binding handles user interactions.
  • Two-Way Binding synchronizes component and view.
  • [(ngModel)] combines Property Binding and Event Binding.
  • Avoid expensive function calls inside templates because they execute during every change detection cycle.
  • Always default to property binding [property]. Only switch to attribute binding [attr.attribute] if Angular throws an error stating that the property is not recognized

docs.title: 📖 What are Directives?
docs.text:
Directives are classes in Angular that allow us to change the behavior or appearance of DOM elements.

They are one of Angular's core building blocks.

Without directives, HTML remains static. Directives make HTML dynamic by adding behavior, modifying styles, or manipulating the DOM.

Angular provides built-in directives and also allows developers to create custom directives.

docs.title: Why Do We Need Directives?
docs.text:
Suppose you want to:

  • Show or hide a section
  • Loop through a list
  • Apply dynamic styles
  • Highlight a field
  • Disable an element
  • Add hover effects

Without directives, you would manually manipulate the DOM using JavaScript.

Angular directives make these tasks declarative and reusable.

docs.title: Types of Directives
docs.text:
Angular has three types of directives.

Directive Type Purpose Example Component Directive Creates a view @Component Structural Directive Adds or removes elements *ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch Attribute Directive Changes appearance or behavior ngClass, ngStyle, Custom Directive

docs.title: Directive Hierarchy
docs.text:
Directive
     │
     ├──────────────┐
     │              │
Component     Attribute Directive
     │
Structural Directive

Every Component is actually a Directive with a template.

docs.title: 1. Component Directive
docs.text:
A Component is a special type of directive.

Unlike other directives, it has:

  • HTML Template
  • CSS
  • TypeScript
  • View

Example

@Component({
    selector:'app-home',
    templateUrl:'./home.component.html'
})
export class HomeComponent{}

docs.title: What are Structural Directives?
docs.text:
Structural directives change the DOM structure.

They can:

  • Create elements
  • Remove elements
  • Repeat elements

Structural directives always begin with *.

docs.title: Why *?
docs.text:
The * is syntactic sugar.

Angular internally converts:

<div *ngIf="isAdmin">

into

<ng-template [ngIf]="isAdmin">
    <div></div>
</ng-template>

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Displays an element only if a condition is true.

Example

isLoggedIn = true;

<div *ngIf="isLoggedIn">
    Welcome User
</div>

Output

Welcome User

If false

The element is completely removed from the DOM.

docs.title: ngIf with else
docs.text:
<div *ngIf="isAdmin; else guest">

Admin

</div>

<ng-template #guest>

Guest User

</ng-template>

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
Difference between

*ngIf

and

display:none

docs.title: ngIf
docs.text: • Removes DOM element

docs.title: display:none
docs.text:
• Element remains in DOM
  • Only hidden

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Repeats an element for every item in a collection.

Example

employees = [
    'John',
    'Mary',
    'David'
];

<li *ngFor="let emp of employees">

{{emp}}

</li>

Output

John

Mary

David

docs.title: Useful Variables
docs.text:
<li *ngFor="let emp of employees;
             index as i;
             first as isFirst;
             last as isLast;
             even as isEven;
             odd as isOdd">

docs.title: trackBy (Very Important)
docs.text:
Without trackBy

Angular recreates every DOM element.

With trackBy

Angular updates only changed rows.

Example

trackById(index:number,item:any){

return item.id;

}

<tr *ngFor="let emp of employees;trackBy:trackById">

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
Why use trackBy?

Answer

Improves performance by preventing unnecessary DOM recreation.

docs.title: ngSwitch
docs.text:
Used when multiple conditions exist.

status='Approved';

<div [ngSwitch]="status">

<div *ngSwitchCase="'Approved'">

Approved

</div>

<div *ngSwitchCase="'Rejected'">

Rejected

</div>

<div *ngSwitchDefault>

Pending

</div>

</div>

docs.title: Attribute Directives
docs.text:
Attribute directives modify an existing HTML element.

They do not create or remove elements.

docs.title: ngClass
docs.text:
Applies CSS classes dynamically.

Example

isActive=true;

<div [ngClass]="{'active':isActive}">

Multiple Classes

<div [ngClass]="{

'active':isActive,

'disabled':isDisabled

}">

docs.title: ngStyle
docs.text:
Applies styles dynamically.

color='red';

<div [ngStyle]="{

'color':color,

'font-size':'20px'

}">

docs.title: Why Create Custom Directives?
docs.text:
Suppose every input field should:

  • Highlight on hover
  • Change border color
  • Display a shadow

Instead of repeating code everywhere, create a reusable directive.

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text:
When the mouse enters an element:

  • Background becomes yellow
  • Text becomes black

When the mouse leaves:

  • Original style returns

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Generate Directive

ng generate directive directives/highlight

Angular creates

highlight.directive.ts

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Directive Code

import {
    Directive,
    ElementRef,
    HostListener,
    Renderer2
} from '@angular/core';

@Directive({
    selector:'[appHighlight]'
})

export class HighlightDirective{

constructor(

private element:ElementRef,

private renderer:Renderer2

){}

@HostListener('mouseenter')

onMouseEnter(){

this.renderer.setStyle(

this.element.nativeElement,

'background',

'yellow'

);

this.renderer.setStyle(

this.element.nativeElement,

'color',

'black'

);

}

@HostListener('mouseleave')

onMouseLeave(){

this.renderer.removeStyle(

this.element.nativeElement,

'background'

);

this.renderer.removeStyle(

this.element.nativeElement,

'color'

);

}

}

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Use Directive

<h2 appHighlight>

Angular Interview Notes

</h2>

<button appHighlight>

Save

</button>

Hovering over any element automatically applies the styles.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
User moves mouse
       │
       ▼
HostListener detects event
       │
       ▼
Directive executes
       │
       ▼
Renderer2 updates DOM
       │
       ▼
UI changes

docs.title: Better Custom Directive Example
docs.text:
Let's make it reusable by allowing the highlight color to be passed as an input.

@Directive({
  selector: '[appHighlight]'
})
export class HighlightDirective {

  @Input() appHighlight = 'yellow';

  constructor(
    private element: ElementRef,
    private renderer: Renderer2
  ) {}

  @HostListener('mouseenter')
  onMouseEnter() {
    this.renderer.setStyle(
      this.element.nativeElement,
      'backgroundColor',
      this.appHighlight
    );
  }

  @HostListener('mouseleave')
  onMouseLeave() {
    this.renderer.removeStyle(
      this.element.nativeElement,
      'backgroundColor'
    );
  }
}

Usage

<p appHighlight>
  Default Yellow
</p>

<p [appHighlight]="'lightgreen'">
  Green Highlight
</p>

<p [appHighlight]="'lightblue'">
  Blue Highlight
</p>

This is much more reusable than hardcoding the color.

docs.title: Why Renderer2?
docs.text:
Instead of

element.nativeElement.style.background='yellow';

Angular recommends

Renderer2

because:

  • Safe DOM manipulation
  • Better security
  • Works with Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
  • Platform independent

docs.title: Real Project Example
docs.text:
In an Employee Management System:

Create a directive that highlights overdue records.

<tr
    [appHighlight]="employee.isExpired ? 'salmon' : 'white'">

Or create a directive to disable buttons based on permissions:

<button appRolePermission="ADMIN">
    Delete Employee
</button>

The directive can check the user's role and enable or disable the button automatically. This avoids repeating permission logic across multiple components.

docs.title: What are Directives?
docs.text: Directives are classes that modify the behavior or appearance of DOM elements.

docs.title: How many types of directives are there?
docs.text:
• Component Directive
  • Structural Directive
  • Attribute Directive

docs.title: Difference between Structural and Attribute Directives
docs.text: Structural Attribute Changes DOM structure Changes appearance or behavior Uses * No * Creates/removes elements Modifies existing elements

docs.title: Why do Structural Directives use *?
docs.text: Because Angular rewrites them into an <ng-template> behind the scenes.

docs.title: Difference between ngIf and hidden/display:none
docs.text: ngIf display:none Removes element from DOM Keeps element in DOM Better for conditional rendering Only hides the element

docs.title: Why use trackBy with ngFor?
docs.text: To improve rendering performance by reusing existing DOM elements instead of recreating them.

docs.title: Why use Renderer2 instead of ElementRef?
docs.text: Renderer2 provides a safe and platform-independent way to manipulate the DOM.

docs.title: Common Interview Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using both *ngIf and *ngFor on the same HTML element.

<!-- Invalid -->
<div *ngIf="show" *ngFor="let emp of employees"></div>

Instead, wrap one directive in an <ng-container>.

<ng-container *ngIf="show">
  <div *ngFor="let emp of employees">
    {{ emp.name }}
  </div>
</ng-container>

❌ Forgetting trackBy for large lists.

❌ Manipulating the DOM directly using nativeElement.style.

Prefer Renderer2.

docs.title: Coding Practice (Highly Recommended)
docs.text:
Implement these custom directives yourself:

  1. Highlight Directive – Change background color on hover.
  2. Auto Focus Directive – Automatically focus an input field.
  3. Uppercase Directive – Convert input text to uppercase while typing.
  4. Only Numbers Directive – Allow only numeric input.
  5. Permission Directive – Show or hide elements based on user roles.
  6. Tooltip Directive – Display a custom tooltip on hover.

These are excellent interview coding exercises and closely resemble tasks you may encounter in real Angular projects.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Directives extend HTML functionality.
  • Angular provides three directive types.
  • Structural directives modify the DOM.
  • Attribute directives modify existing elements.
  • Components are specialized directives with templates.
  • Use trackBy with *ngFor for better performance.
  • Use Renderer2 instead of directly manipulating the DOM.
  • Custom directives help eliminate duplicate UI behavior and improve code reusability.
